description: Hello everyone, I’m Harsh Unagar. I’ve been fascinated by interstellar space and astronomy since I was a kid. This year, I discovered the NASA Space Apps Challenge and decided to participate. I’m participating alone, and I’m completely fine with that. I’m here because I genuinely love space, want to learn, explore, and build something meaningful while experiencing that childhood interest all over again.
summary: Lunar Mission Browser answers a planner's first two questions about the Moon's south pole: which landing site, and which month? Pick any of fifteen sites and a date, and the page answers in words first. It says whether the site is sunlit, how much power a solar panel makes, whether Earth is above the horizon, and whether the radio link to Earth is open. Under the answer sits a 360-degree view of the real skyline from NASA's LOLA terrain data, with the paths of the Sun and Earth drawn across it. A 30-day timeline shows power, Earth visibility and Deep Space Network windows. Three sites compare side by side, a table ranks all fifteen for the same month, and a strip shows the next two years. Every position is checked against JPL Horizons. The terrain and orbit data stay behind that answer, so nobody needs planning software to read it. The page is free, works on a phone, and needs no sign-in.
details:
What it does

The browser is for one decision: where and when to land near the lunar south pole so that a lander has sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for its radio. Near the pole the Sun stays low and Earth sits near the horizon, so a hill a few kilometres away can cut off either one. The page shows which, for any site and any date from 2020 to 2050.

  1. Choose a site and a date. There are fifteen sites:
    A custom point anywhere from 85°S to the pole also works.
    • the IM-1 and IM-2 landings;
    • five of NASA's Artemis III candidate regions;
    • four published candidate landing sites inside the other regions;
    • Shackleton crater, two high-light ridge points and the pole itself.
  2. Read the answer. Four tiles say, in plain words:
    • whether the Sun is up and how much of its disc clears the skyline;
    • the power a Sun-tracking panel makes;
    • whether Earth is in view, and how much of it is lit;
    • whether a link to Earth is open now, and why or why not.
  3. See the skyline. A 360° panorama of the real skyline shows where the Sun and Earth move across it. A 3D map of the south pole and a ground view let you stand at the site.
  4. Plan over time.
    • A 30-day timeline gives power, Earth visibility and direct-to-Earth windows.
    • It sums up the month: sunlit share, mean power, energy made, the battery needed to last the longest night, and the longest blackout.
    • "Find next" jumps to the next sunrise or the next open link.
  5. Compare.
    • Up to three sites side by side.
    • A table ranks all fifteen for the same 30 days.
    • A strip of 24 windows shows the next two years for the chosen site.
  6. Share and print. The address holds the whole view, so a link shows a colleague exactly the same thing. Printing gives a one-page report per site. The data exports as CSV.

Mission settings. These change every number on the page:

  • mast height (ground, 2 m or 10 m);
  • the network (NASA's Deep Space Network, or DSN plus ESA's Estrack);
  • the antenna elevation floor;
  • panel size and efficiency;
  • the lander's power draw.

Fourteen controls. The challenge names over-complicated tools as the problem, so the page keeps to 14 controls and three steps to the main answer. An automated test fails if either number grows.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth positions. Computed in the browser, with no server:
    Against JPL Horizons (DE441, the Moon's mean-Earth frame) over 2024–2035, the worst error is 0.0066° for the Sun and 0.0038° for Earth. The stated tolerance is 0.05°.
    • the Moon's position from Meeus's lunar theory;
    • the Earth–Moon barycentre from JPL's "Approximate Positions of the Planets";
    • the Moon's orientation from the IAU rotation model.
  • Terrain. Each site's skyline is the highest terrain angle along 360 rays out to 150 km, with the Moon's curvature included. It uses LOLA's 120 m and 240 m polar elevation grids.
    The ground view stands on LOLA 10 m and 5 m south-pole elevation models from NASA Goddard's PGDA. LRO camera mosaics lie over the ground.
    The skylines were checked against the published illumination study by Gläser et al. (NASA NTRS 20170007365).
  • Power. Power is the share of the solar disc above the skyline, times 1361 W/m², at the Moon's real distance from the Sun. Earth's shadow is included, so lunar eclipses show up. Eclipse times were checked against NASA's Five Millennium Canon of Lunar Eclipses.
  • Communication. The page finds when the Moon is above each Deep Space Network antenna's elevation floor, and when Earth is above the site's own skyline. Antenna positions come from DSN document 810-005.
    Over 2024–2035 it gives 98.644% coverage for the DSN alone and 100% with ESA's stations added. Both figures match Horizons' hourly elevations.
    The page also says when a gap is the network's and when it is the terrain's.
  • Speed. The 30-day and two-year sums run in a web worker, so the page stays responsive on a phone.

Testing

Every number on the page is checked by an automated test against a primary source, mostly JPL Horizons runs kept with the code. The project has 81 automated test scripts, most of them run in a real browser with Playwright. They cover:

  • the numbers;
  • the 14-control limit;
  • printing, sharing and phones;
  • accessibility.

A change is deployed only when its tests pass.

Who it is for

Mission planners get a quick first look at sites and months, with a link to share and a printed report. Teachers get a lesson on the site's teachers' page that uses the browser, with a worksheet and an answer key in English and Hindi. Anyone else gets the answer in words before the numbers, inside Orrery Space, a free 3D Solar System that also has a Moon explorer.

Tools, languages and hardware

  • Code: TypeScript, built with Vite.
  • 3D: Three.js for the 3D map and the ground view.
  • Data tools: Node.js scripts that read NASA's terrain products by HTTP range requests and turn them into small files for the browser. The 10 m terrain files total about 20 MB, loaded only when a site is opened.
  • Tests: Playwright.
  • Hosting: a static website with no server code, so it costs almost nothing to run.
  • Hardware: one Windows laptop. The page runs on any phone or computer with a web browser.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

What to select: pick the options that cover:

  • code;
  • text and documentation;
  • translation;
  • audio (the demo's narration).

If the list has separate options for images or video, leave them unticked. No picture in the demo video or on /lunar/ was made by AI: every frame is a screen recording of the live page.

Rules the form sets, and how the project meets them:

Form's rule

How it is met

Audio: acknowledge SI in descriptive text and metadata

Text: this disclosure. Metadata: the video's comment and description tags say "Narration is an AI-generated voice (Chatterbox TTS)".

Images and videos: a visible SI watermark

Does not apply: the demo's picture is real screen recordings, not AI-generated.

Code and data: acknowledge SI in descriptive text and metadata

Text: this disclosure.

No NASA branding (logos, flags, mission identifiers)

No NASA logo or insignia appears in the video or on the page. NASA is named only as the source of the data.
